Repository: /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin (OrcaSlicer fork "JusPrin"). Work in your own git worktree, based on the branch `claude/no-save-prompts` (local, unpushed, in worktree .claude/worktrees/hungry-bartik-ceb424; commits d33fb306c9 and 7852470aff are the relevant ones) or on origin/jusprin-newui once that branch is merged. Do not touch the main checkout or another session's worktree.

Background. On 2026-09-29 Kenneth decided JusPrin never asks a person to save or discard: autosave keeps the work and version history is the way back. On 2026-10-14 the printer nozzle change was changed to follow that rule: `change_named_printer_nozzle` in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Printers/NamedPrinters.cpp drops the project printer's unsaved edits only after a caller-supplied step (`keep_unsaved_edits`, which pins an autosave version; supplied by ShellController through PrinterPanel::Callbacks) has saved them to version history. If that step is missing or fails, the nozzle is not changed and the function returns the message "The unsaved changes to this printer couldn't be saved to the project's history, so the nozzle was not changed." The printer panel's `printer_change` tool (PrinterConversation::change in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterConversation.cpp) turns that into a plain tool error with code `change_failed`.

The open question. Kenneth said this behavior is wrong too, without saying what is right. Today the agent improvises: the printer prompt (src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts) has guidance after a failed connection and for refused settings, but nothing about `change_failed` from `printer_change`. It is NOT an OrcaSlicer confirmation (warning code `skipped_confirmation`, returned by settings_preview_patch for a valid patch that applies as sent), and must not become one: the nozzle must never change while the edits exist nowhere else.

What to do: investigate and propose the right handling, for example whether the failure should be retried automatically, carry a distinct error code and recovery steps in the result, change how the panel presents it, or get one sentence of prompt guidance (prompt text is restructured by another task, so coordinate before editing printerInstructions.ts). Read agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md (printer panel section) and agent-docs/jusprin/autosave-version-history.md first. Reproduce the failure path with the shell harness (`JusPrinShellHarness --printer-setup`; checks named nozzle_change_whose_keeper_fails_leaves_unsaved_edits and nozzle_panel_*). Do not call any live model without Kenneth approving a specific batch. Write your proposal for Kenneth in plain English: what happens today, the options with consequences, your recommendation. Do not push.

result.output:
# Local autosave and version history

JusPrin saves authored projects in the application data directory under
`jusprin/projects/<project-id>/`. The project ID is independent of the source
filename. Opening an external 3MF or model imports it into a managed draft;
autosave never overwrites the source. **Saved** means the printable
project checkpoint and the current JusPrin document are durable. A 3MF is written
to a user-selected path only through **Export project 3MF…**. A copied 3MF does
not include local versions, conversations, or attachments.

The project header's actions menu exposes the save state, version history,
recent local projects, and export. Version history restores an earlier model
and its effective project settings. The native window title shows the managed
project name and the same save state as the header. Orca's dirty asterisk
does not represent whether the local project has been saved. Before restoring,
JusPrin saves and pins
the current version, then records the restore as a new version, so the prior
state remains available. Each older timestamp has a separate Restore button;
clicking the timestamp does nothing, and Restore asks for confirmation. A blank authored project gets one empty baseline
version so it can be reopened; later document edits do not add versions. A
first Agent model operation pins that baseline as its before-version.
Conversation, intent, plan, region descriptions,
audit, and completed print records remain in the current document. Restoring a
model does not undo physical prints or change global printer facts. Agent
mutations save and pin their actual
before-state, then link an after-version and outcome in an operation record.

## Storage and recovery contract

The restoration rules above describe ordinary Version history. **Restore and
resume** is a separate chat transition. Each active chat keeps a checkpoint
with a model-version reference, matching print intent, plan and region
annotations, and a structured setup summary. Browsing an older chat does not
change the working project. Resuming it saves and pins the outgoing state,
restores the model and matching planning fields, and activates that chat only
after the new document is durable. Other conversations, audit and print
records, and global printer facts remain. This does not add a full project-
document copy to model versions or make document edits create model versions.
Ordinary Version history remains model-only and does not activate an older
chat. An interrupted chat transition leaves a durable pending marker and
blocks that managed project for explicit recovery on restart.

Each model version has Orca backup-format metadata and a manifest of object
resources. It has no copy of the project document. Unchanged object resources are referenced rather
than serialized again. Changed objects are serialized with Orca's split-model
writer into immutable ZIP resources. A renamed object can reuse its resource;
materialization relabels its entry for Orca's native restore loader. Metadata
and each resource are checked for required entries and geometry. The live
Orca backup directory and an imported source file are never version-store
dependencies.

All project records advance one `current-state.json` document without creating
a model version. The document is atomically replaced after 1.5 seconds without
a change, or within 15 seconds during a continuous stream. Agent and project
boundaries wait for the write. Attachments are written once before their
document references become durable; operation records linking before/after
versions are committed once at the operation boundary. A model checkpoint
ensures the current document is durable before it publishes a new `HEAD`.

## Save classification

The autosave controller observes two independent kinds of change. Native
geometry, transforms, paint, plates, and effective project settings can change
what an earlier printable project reconstructs and therefore create a model
version. Document changes, including streamed Agent messages, drafts, intent,
plans, region descriptions, audit records, and print facts, update only the
current document. `docRevision` is a signal to coalesce that write; neither
it nor document contents participate in model-version equality. A workspace
event can prompt a model check, but cannot make unchanged checkpoint content
into a new version.

A single writer owns each project through an OS file lock. It writes and
flushes the current document and changed resources before publishing a version directory,
then atomically replaces `HEAD` with the ordered committed-version index.
POSIX also synchronizes containing directories; Windows flushes individual
files and uses `MoveFileExW` with `MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH`. Restart discards
unfinished staging, unindexed versions, unreachable resources, and old
disposable restore directories. If saving
fails, the current model stays open, the header reports a local save failure,
and the next save retries it. Project replacement is blocked until the live
state is saved. Explicit export validates a temporary 3MF before replacing
its destination.

Older projects may still contain `Auxiliaries/JusPrin/state.json` and a
recovery mirror. On first adoption, JusPrin reads that state and copies its
attachments to the managed store; it does not delete the old source. Once a
managed version exists, local state is authoritative. Reopening a copied
external 3MF with an already managed identity forks a new project identity.
When a file opened as a project matches a saved project, JusPrin asks whether
to create another project or open the existing one directly. A project
remembers the file it was opened from (`openedFrom`) and that file's MD5 then
(`openedDigest`) in each version manifest: a .3mf from its project path, a model
file the agent's `project_open` opened as a new project from the path it gave.
Every way a person opens a .3mf asks, because the check sits in
`Plater::load_project` (File > Open Project, recent files, Finder, drops); the
agent's `project_open` returns the question as `opened_before` and takes the
answer as `openedBefore`. A file whose MD5 differs is a likely new export, so
the question says so and defaults to a new project; otherwise it defaults to
the saved one. Versions saved before 2026-10-14 have no digest and are asked
about as unchanged. Importing a file into a project never asks. If several
projects match, it continues the current one when it came from that file;
otherwise it opens the most recently updated match.
Earlier local versions with `state.json` and a model-bound document sidecar
remain readable; the first new document write upgrades them to the independent
current-document format without rewriting historical versions.
Recent projects appear on Home and in the header menu. Selecting one
opens its managed version even when its imported source file has been removed.
The most recently authored local project resumes on startup.

## Chosen defaults and limits

- The controller checks a lightweight native state signature every 2 seconds
  and waits 1.5 seconds after an observed model edit before starting a background
  model save. Document changes use the coalesced state write described above;
  they never call Orca's 3MF exporter. An unchanged project does not run the
  exporter. Project replacement and Agent boundaries save synchronously.
- While the JusPrin shell owns managed autosave, Orca's automatic backup timer
  and object-mesh backup cache are suspended. The configured backup interval is
  left intact and resumes if the shell is detached. Manual 3MF export remains
  available.
- Retention aims for at most 200 versions and 4 GiB per project. These are
  soft limits: the current version, pinned versions, and Agent operation
  references survive even when they exceed the budget. Unreferenced object
  resources and attachments are removed after the retained index is durable.
- A support, seam, color, or fuzzy paint edit can serialize the whole painted
  object because Orca stores triangle paint with its mesh. The coherence
  spike measured about 31 MB and 6.7 seconds of worker time for a large paint
  edit; this is a fixture measurement, not a latency guarantee.
- History is local to this application data directory. There is no portable
  history export or automatic cloud synchronization.

## Verification

The native workspace harness checks the current document across historical
model restores, selective resources, all four paint
channels, empty restore, corrupt and missing resource rejection, export
replacement, locks, retention, and attachment reachability. The shell harness
checks streamed replies without per-word model exports, legacy adoption,
failed-save behavior, restore, restart, and Agent
boundaries. Separate process tests stop publication after resources, version,
and `HEAD`, then verify recovery in a fresh process. These checks run on macOS;
Windows and Linux runtime behavior still needs platform verification before
those builds are released.

## Tool budget and tool shape

The limit on the number of tools comes from how much the model has to load on each turn. It does not come from how much the app can do. The rules in this section rest on this evidence:

- OpenAI's function-calling guidance keeps fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn and defers the rest.
- Anthropic's [tool-writing guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) asks for a few tools aimed at high-impact workflows. It names "tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints" as the common error.
- A [domain-oriented MCP study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.22063v1) measured three interfaces. A generic interface of thin tools scored below raw SQL. Tools shaped around the domain scored far above both.
- The "god tool", one tool that dispatches many unrelated actions through a single `action` parameter, is a documented anti-pattern.

The current five-tool MCP catalog measures about 1.9 KB per definition, and two thirds of that is output schema.

**How tools are loaded for now.** Both adapters load every registered tool on every turn. The in-app adapter sends the full function list with each request, and MCP `tools/list` returns the whole catalog. This is the simplest behaviour that is correct. It also keeps the tools array byte-identical through a chat, and OpenAI's prompt cache depends on exactly that. The budget is 20 definitions per turn. Going over 20 does not block anything. It is the point at which we start watching the measurements. The live regression test records definition bytes, input tokens, and cached tokens for each request. The journey catalog below goes over 20 definitions from its first milestone. We accept that until those measurements show the model selecting wrong tools or running short of context.

**The baseline, measured on Windows against the live app.**

| After milestone | In-app definitions | In-app bytes | MCP definitions | MCP bytes | MCP bytes through the offline helper recipe |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| M0 | 7 | 3,145 | 5 | 3,147 | |
| M1 | 11 | 6,482 | 9 | 6,915 | |
| M2 | 18 | 12,721 | 16 | 13,911 | 13,894 |
| M3 | 20 | 19,331 | 21 | 22,661 | 22,639 |
| M4 | 20 | 21,594 | 21 | 24,923 | 24,901 |
| M5 | 25 | 29,148 | 26 | 33,013 | |

The M5 figure for MCP was read over two `tools/list` pages.

The `--live-agent` regression test, run at M0 and at M1, shows what those definitions cost in tokens. The first request of a conversation gets nothing from the cache and pays for the whole catalog: 803 tokens at M0 and 1,733 at M1. So four more definitions cost about 930 tokens, paid once. Every later request in the same conversation came back 77 to 92 per cent cached (at M1, 5,864 input tokens, of which 5,376 were cached). That is because the tools array is byte-identical through a chat, and the cache depends on that. At M2, the same test made eleven requests that took 2,875 to 6,763 input tokens, with 42 to 91 per cent cached. None of the eleven started with an empty cache, because an earlier run on the same day had already cached the shared beginning of the prompt. So that run did not measure the uncached cost at M2.

The conclusion is that a definition adds cost to the *first* request of each conversation, not to every turn. That is why going over the budget only makes us look at the measurements and does not block a tool. Two things would change this conclusion: a catalog so large that the first request of every conversation is expensive by itself, or transcripts that show the model choosing the wrong tool. Watch for both. Neither has appeared yet.

**The printer panel follows the same rule with its own set of tools.** The printer panel on Home runs its own conversation, `PrinterConversation`. That conversation is offered the five printer tools and the four settings tools. The list is the same in every mode (Add, Change, or Connect), so it stays byte-identical through a conversation and between conversations of the same mode.

What a call may do depends on the conversation. `PrinterConversation::preflight_tool` refuses every call that is not allowed, before any card is shown, with an error that says where to go instead. The rules are:

- Finding and adding a printer (`printer_identify`, `printer_add`) is allowed only in an Add conversation. A Change or Connect conversation is about a printer the person already has. An add there would save another printer and move the conversation onto it.
- `printer_change` is allowed only on the printer the conversation is about, once there is one. When the project uses that printer and it has unsaved edits, the nozzle changes only after those edits are saved to the project's version history (`change_named_printer_nozzle` takes the step that saves them, and refuses without it); they are then dropped and listed in `discarded`. The panel's coordinator also saves a version before the call, as the project's agent pane does for any change to the project.
- The connection tools are allowed only once there is a saved printer.
- The settings tools are allowed only with `scope: "printer"`, on the printer the conversation is about.

A Change conversation may be about a stock profile (one that ships with OrcaSlicer) that the project has selected. That happens when the person chooses Printer settings… in the header on a project that uses a stock profile. In that case, changes to the nozzle and to the connection are refused with `stock_profile`. Changes to settings are saved as a copy of the profile, and the conversation follows that copy from then on (`PrinterConversation::tool_settled`). A Change conversation is never turned into an Add conversation. The code that opens a Change conversation checks that the printer is there, and shows OrcaSlicer's error dialog when it is not.

The header's filament chat uses the same panel (`PrinterPanel::open_filament`). It is offered the four settings tools and nothing else, and it gets no project state. It has its own instructions. The page writes them in `AgentUI/src/filamentInstructions.ts` and sends them with `filament_instructions`. The page writes them from the facts the app sends as the session part of the panel's state (`PrinterPanel::filament_session_json`): the preset's name, its slot and material, and, for a stock filament, the copy that a change is saved as. The preflight check for this chat allows the settings tools only with `scope: "filament"` on that preset. It refuses an apply that has no `persistAs`, with `not_saved`, because the chat is gone when it closes. When a copy is saved in the preset's place, the chat is about that copy from then on, and the page writes the instructions again for the copy. Until 2026-09-29 the filament chat ran on the project assistant's instructions and tools. With those, the model read "make the nozzle 5 degrees hotter" as a request to print. In another run it set 205 °C when the value was 220 °C, without reading the value first.

We do not give each mode a different tool list, for two reasons. The conversation has to refuse disallowed calls anyway, whatever list the model is shown. And the way to restrict tools while keeping the list stable (`tool_choice` with `allowed_tools`) exists only on some providers. We would reconsider if transcripts showed the model reaching for a refused tool and then failing to recover. `tests/printer_prompt` measures this with the `change-add-another` case.

Two past changes explain the current design:

- Until 2026-09-23 the panel offered one tool per mode (7f66e75b07). The reason was to keep a printer lookup from clearing the pinned card of the printer a Change session was about. That card is gone (4d4f9e466b). Offering one tool per step also left an Add conversation with no tool to connect the printer it had just added (8334b3395b).
- On 2026-09-28 three tools were removed (b60fc2d8e6): `printer_manual_setup`, `printer_manual_connection` and `printer_setup_finish`. These were the tools that opened a window or closed the panel. OrcaSlicer's full printer list and a printer's settings are still reachable from the panel's own buttons, and the person closes the panel.

The app decides which tools are offered. The page writes the text: `AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` holds the instructions, and `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts` holds the notes the model reads after a tap. If a turn arrives before the page has written its instructions, the app refuses the turn. It does not send the turn with the project assistant's prompt. The instructions for an Add conversation carry the whole printer list, about 28 KB. That text is always the same and sits at the start of the instructions, so it is cached. No printer conversation carries the project: no workspace state goes into the turn, and none goes into a tool result.

**Deferral, when the measurements say so.** Deferral means the model first sees only a short index and loads a tool's full definition when it needs it. Use the deferral feature that the model platform provides. Never write our own mechanism for switching tools in and out. For the in-app Agent, the platform feature is OpenAI's `tool_search` with `defer_loading: true` on the Responses API. It is documented for `gpt-5.4` and later. Whether it works on the pinned `gpt-5.4-mini` has not been verified. On the MCP side, clients defer by themselves, as Claude Code does. Tools would be deferred one toolset at a time (toolsets are the named groups in the candidate catalog), and OpenAI recommends fewer than ten functions per namespace. Do not build a tool that enables a toolset by rewriting the tools array. Every switch would break the prompt cache.

**Shape each tool as a domain operation.** A tool does one thing that a slicer user has a name for: place an object, lay out the plates, mark a region, set up the printer. Do not wrap each OrcaSlicer function in its own tool. Do not build a tool that interprets a list of unrelated commands. One operation may have several optional facets, as long as each facet has its own type and the tool rejects facets that conflict.

**Batch only where items share a shape.** Good examples are a list of setting changes, a list of intent fields, a list of annotations, and a list of layout rows with one row per object. A list that mixes transforms, imports, and deletes is the god tool described above. It is refused.

**Fold reads into sections and detail levels before adding a read tool.** A new read tool is justified in only two cases. Either its inputs are of a different kind (a search over a large catalog, an analysis of one object, a report on a sliced plate), or its result is an image.

**Let call logs decide consolidation.** If transcripts show that two tools are always called together, consider merging them. If two facets of one tool are never used together, consider splitting them. Make these decisions from eval evidence, not from a design discussion.

**Output schemas are not advertised over MCP.** No client was shown to use them, and they were two thirds of the catalog. `tools/list` no longer carries `outputSchema`. `validate_output` still checks every successful MCP result, so a result that breaks its contract still fails with a visible error. We measured the effect on one build, with the recipe near the end of this guide. With five tools, the catalog went from 9,723 bytes to 3,141, which is from about 2,430 tokens to 785. Only the MCP side saves anything. The in-app adapter has always sent `input_schema` as `parameters` and nothing else, so an in-app turn never carried output schemas. Restore the field only for a client that is shown to read it.

## Errors should teach the next valid call

When an invalid state is expected, handle it with ordinary control flow and return a structured error. Do not throw an exception. An error should say what the problem is and include only the data the Agent needs to correct the call.

The MCP errors today include `invalid_arguments`, `cancelled`, `workspace_unavailable` and `stale_workspace`. The MCP adapter converts the app's native `stale_revision` and `stale_id` into `stale_workspace`, with the expected and the current session and revision in the details. It converts `unavailable_operation` into `workspace_unavailable`. Protocol errors at the transport level are separate JSON-RPC errors. Native error codes and MCP error codes do not have to be spelled the same.

The settings tools return these correction details, each limited in size:

- unknown setting: the canonical code `unknown_setting`, the original key, and a short `suggestions` list;
- invalid enum value: the key, a diagnostic message, and the valid values in `allowed`;
- value out of range: the key, a diagnostic message, and the `min`/`max` bounds. Units are available from the setting's metadata;
- incompatible settings: the keys that conflict, and OrcaSlicer's reason;
- stale call: the expected and the current session/revision, plus an instruction to read again;
- unavailable operation: the requested scope has no active preset or target.

A failure that should be impossible (a broken invariant) must stay visible to diagnostics and to Sentry. Catch an error at the boundary between two layers only to recover from it, to translate a known error, or to add context that is essential.

name: background-bash-timeout-kills-builds
description: "A run_in_background Bash build dies at the tool timeout (ninja prints \"interrupted by user\", exit 130); launch long builds with nohup and watch the log instead"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 8c1e8dd3-1475-48e9-9398-2d5eaa424bab
  modified: 2026-09-14T19:01:34.576Z
---

A `cmake --build` started with the Bash tool's `run_in_background` is still
bound by that call's `timeout` (default 120 s, max 600 s). When it fires the
build log ends with `ninja: build stopped: interrupted by user.` and `exit=130`,
which looks like a human Ctrl-C but is the harness. Seen 2026-09-14 on a
725-step JusPrin rebuild.

**Why:** the notification says "completed" and the log shows no compiler
error, so it is easy to misread as a finished build; the changed files had not
compiled at all.

**How to apply:** for anything longer than a few minutes, start it detached
(`nohup sh -c "cmake --build … > log 2>&1; echo exit=\$? >> log" & disown`),
then arm a Monitor on the log that reports progress and the `exit=` line. Check
`grep -c '<file>.cpp.o' log` before trusting the result. Related:
[[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]], [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

description: "Reproduce any JusPrin tool behaviour without a live model in about 20 s per run: shell harness --manual-mcp plus tests/mcp/probe.py call(); two traps (leaked harness from `cd && cmd &`, slice_start on an unchanged sliced plate)"

Used 2026-10-12 for the spiral vase investigation (branch `claude/spiral-vase-writable`).

**Recipe.** Start `build/arm64/tests/shell/Release/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness --manual-mcp <scratch dir>` with `HOME=<scratch home>`, wait for `HARNESS MCP FIXTURE READY` on stderr (about 15 s), read the URL from `<scratch dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`, then call tools with `probe.call(urlsplit(url), "tools/call", {"name": ..., "arguments": ...})` imported from `tests/mcp/probe.py`. The fixture is two plates, one 20 mm box each, Bambu X1C 0.4, "Bambu PLA Basic @BBL X1C", "0.20mm Standard @BBL X1C", the same presets as Kenneth's live tests. Another session's harness can run at the same time; the port falls back from 47301 and the discovery file is per data dir.

**Trap 1: leaked harness.** In a script, `cd "$S" && nohup harness ... &` makes `$!` the subshell, so `kill $!` leaves the harness running, and the next run's `rm -rf <fixture>` fails with "Directory not empty". Write `cd "$S"; nohup harness ... &`. Check with `pgrep -fl "<worktree>.*JusPrinShellHarness"` before finishing.

**Trap 2: slice_start on a sliced, unchanged plate.** The fixture's plate 1 starts sliced. `slice_start` on it (with or without `wait`) left it reported `sliced: false`, `slice_report` `valid: false`, and with `wait: true` the probe saw the stream close with no reply. Orca's log says "background process in idle state, use previous result". Change a setting first, then slice. Not investigated further.

**Timings on this Mac, Release config, load 30 to 40:** fresh worktree build of `jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs agent_bridge_tests workspace_contract_tests setting_display_tests shell_integration_harness` was 905 steps in about 14 min; the shell harness default regression (549 checks) about 2 min; the workspace adapter harness (972 checks) under 1 min. See [[jusprin-worktree-build]], [[live-test-built-app-on-mac]].

**Seeding a preset (2026-10-12).** `--manual-mcp` does not wipe its directory at start, so a user preset written to `<fixture>/user/default/machine/<name>.json` before launch (keys `from: User`, `inherits`, `name`, `printer_settings_id`, `version`, plus the values under test) is loaded and can be named as a settings `target.preset`. A Python driver that starts the harness with `subprocess.Popen` and terminates it in `finally` avoids Trap 1.
